findings.claim: Nocturnal autumn passage over the mid-latitude US is happening earlier.
findings.scope: 78 US weather-radar stations between 37°N and 50°N, 1995-2025. Not the whole continent: the southern bands carry a step change at 2012 that four candidate explanations have failed to account for.
findings.caveat: The radar measures aerial biomass, not birds — it cannot separate birds from bats from insects. Bats in particular are not excluded.
supporting: Reproduces a published result on its own window before extending it.
Survives four break specifications, a mid-winter placebo and a permutation null.
Unchanged when the speed weighting is removed from the metric.
Unchanged when the non-bird nights are deleted outright.

findings.claim: There is no single global poleward shift in fish distribution — surveys disagree even in its direction.
findings.value: median -0.011 °latitude per decade across 2,240 species-survey pairs
findings.scope: 29 harmonised scientific bottom-trawl surveys, North America and Europe, on consistently sampled cells only.
findings.caveat: A pooled median hides the variation worth predicting: individual surveys reach -0.22 and +0.26 °latitude per decade in opposite directions. The unit of analysis has to be the species in its region, not the ocean.

findings.claim: The autumn signal is not drifting from birds towards insects — what the radar measures in 2025 means what it meant in 1995.
findings.scope: 2,193,560 station-night wind samples, 1995-2025, from an independent regional reanalysis rather than from the radar.
findings.caveat: Spring behaves differently: its airspeed rose, which is either a real change or migrants flying higher than the fixed wind level assumes. Separating those needs the vertical radar profiles. Spring carries no trend claim here either way.
supporting: Mean autumn airspeed sits in the range for migrating songbirds, not insects.
A 2012 discontinuity in the dataset's own rain filtering was traced, and ruled out as weather using independent precipitation data.

findings.claim: Everything above is northern-hemisphere. The data that can measure change and the data that covers the globe are, so far, different data.
findings.value: 0.0% of the radar record and 0.0% of the survey record lie south of the equator
findings.scope: Every source in this project that has a usable time axis.
findings.caveat: Inherited rather than chosen — long digitised radar and trawl series exist where they were funded — but it bounds every claim here to the northern temperate zone, and no model trained on it should be trusted elsewhere without being tested there first.
